webTitle: Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment | Sidney Blumenthal

fields.headline: Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment
fields.trailText: The president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationale
fields.bodyText: Trumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedly told the annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as the Pirate King was not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later. Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th-century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources. Describing his actions as some version of colonialism grants him a more orderly and coherent method than he possesses. His pillaging bears not the slightest resemblance to the highly organized administration of Queen Victoria’s British empire. Trump’s predation is calculated to wreck the long-established arrangements of international trade, law and cooperation created after the second world war and the fall of colonial empires, whose guidelines he sees as obstructing his own profit and power. Obsessed with his fortune hunting, he couldn’t care less about the political consequences for ill-fated Republican candidates in the midterm elections who must face the music for the harm he is doing to their states. They are the least of his collateral damage. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, offered the most succinct critique of Trump’s intent to usurp the sovereignty of countries in order to make them turn over their wealth to him. Carney said: “Canada is a sovereign, independent nation. We are not a target to be bullied, nor are we a client state to be subordinated … We will not sign an agreement that sacrifices our basic sovereignty, undermines our legal system, or cedes control over our foreign trade to Washington.” He called Trump’s demands a “last-minute power play intended to reduce Canada to an economic subsidiary”. Trump’s ultimatum abrogated the legal foundation of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which he himself had signed in 2020. He had previously demeaned Carney as the “governor” of Canada. Now, adopting his characteristic pose as victim, Trump claimed Canada had been “ripping off the United States for years” and were among “worst” nations to “deal with”.. “They feel entitled and will be entitled no longer … It’s time to teach Canada you can’t do this anymore…. Someone should get these clowns to fall in line.” Carney replied that Canada was “at war” and would adopt “counter-measures”, tariffs of its own. “America,” he said, “has changed … If Washington wants to trade, they must come to the table as equals.” Trump’s answer was to issue an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, the reflexive branding of the real estate operator. The White House put out AI-generated videos of Trump kicking over a sign reading “Lake Ontario” and replacing it with a new one, “Lake America”, and another with a squadron of ducks all with Trump’s hairdo and armed with machine guns patrolling the shore of “Lake America” to the theme music of Hawaii Five-O. The implied invocation of the Marx brothers’ farce of the ludicrous country of Freedonia nonsensically going to war, Duck Soup, seems lost on the busy beavers of Trump’s slop. Trump’s method has been consistent since he leveraged a mineral resource deal out of Ukraine in April 2025 at a weak point in its conflict with Russia. Rather than pressure Putin, Trump’s agents disguised as diplomats, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate pal Steve Witkoff, the Rosencrantz and Guildenstern of Trump’s imperialism, stand by to negotiate post-sanctions deals on his behalf. Venezuela became Trump’s template for his piratical adventures. After swooping in on 3 January to capture its strongman, Nicolás Maduro, Trump promised a transition to democratic elections and that the US would play a custodial role over Venezuelan oil for the benefit of its people. Not long after Trump grabbed Maduro, he declared he needed to acquire Greenland and threatened a tariff war against Denmark and European allies to “get Greenland, including right, title and ownership”. “We probably won’t get anything unless I decide to use excessive strength and force, where we would be frankly unstoppable. But I won’t do that,” Trump said, adding, “I don’t have to use force,” and “I don’t want to use force.” He relented momentarily on 21 January after he claimed he had reached a “framework” agreement to negotiate over natural resources, though he subsequently sent preposterous agents into Greenland to stir up a quixotic annexation movement to no avail. A month later, he bombed Iran. Trump stated that his true inspiration for the Iran war was the Venezuelan model in a post on 11 June: “At some point in the not too distant future, we will … assume total control of their Oil and Gas Markets, much like we have with Venezuela, which is working out brilliantly for both Venezuela and the United States of America.” On 31 August, Trump announced that the US would take a stake in 17 oilfields in partnership with North American Blue Energy Partners, controlled by a Venezuelan oilman, Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt was briefly detained in Britain, which was reportedly linked to a Swiss warrant on suspicion of money laundering. Betancourt has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any offenses. The Swiss warrant was withdrawn in May and he became a Trump associate. The Trump administration has already claimed to have received proceeds of $500m from oil sales, initially deposited in an account in Qatar. When the congressman Sean Casten of Illinois and the senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland wrote a letter requesting information, the administration shifted the money to an opaque account managed by the treasury department. In an article published in June by the Council on Foreign Relations, “The U.S. Took Over Venezuela’s Oil Industry. Where Has All the Money Gone?”, Roxana Vigil, a former treasury department expert, observed that in dealing with the “same corrupt regime, different leader … the Trump administration has provided almost no information on the system it has established to sell Venezuelan oil, collect the revenue, and use the funds”. The countries whose sovereignty, self-interest and rule of law Trump has struck include the United States. His assault on Canada has sent a shock through the whole US economy. The state most affected economically, Michigan, shares with Canada one of the most integrated industrial relationships in the world. More than 38% of Michigan’s exports go to Canada, the Detroit-Windsor corridor handles 25% of all US-Canada trade, and Trump’s tariffs immediately threaten 260,000 jobs with an immensely damaging multiplier effect. As of March, his tariffs had already caused estimated losses of $35bn to automakers. The average cost per Michigan household is estimated to be $5,619 in added expenses due to tariff-induced price increases. Trump’s tariffs have effectively hamstrung the Republican candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, leaving him with the Hobson’s choice of either inciting Trump’s rage or submitting to his whim. Rogers has decided to take the latter course. He has called Trump’s economic policies “masterful”. When JD Vance came to the state, Rogers praised the administration. “The impact you have had on our state is phenomenal,” he said. Rogers hurls language about “extremism” against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that substitutes for discussing Trump’s economic fiasco. Rogers is performing the kind of self-abasing fealty to Trump that Trump wishes he would receive from Carney. If only Rogers were the prime minister of Canada, there would be no trouble about “independence”. Vladimir Lenin, in his 1917 tract, Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism, argued in his dogmatic and overdetermined style that imperialism at the turn of the 20th century represented the integration of monopoly, finance and industrial capital, with the great powers dividing the world into colonies, and their conflict precipitating the first world war. In Trump’s imaginarium, he views himself as omnipotent and omniscient. When the world isn’t pliable, he must resort to greater force to reassure himself that the world acknowledges his self-image. The more he meets resistance to his fixed idea, the more pressure he must exert. He finds himself in a vicious cycle. His power hemorrhages, US power dissipates and he spins in a whirlpool. Trump’s Venezuelan paradigm, whose conditions cannot be replicated, have quickly descended into questionable business deals. Failed from the start of his Iran war, his pursuit of “total control” recedes over the horizon. His clash with Canada has been confronted with Carney’s fierce defiance. Trump’s quest for a new field to conquer has landed him in yet another quagmire. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” said Carney. In the meantime, Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than they echo Marx and Lenin: “Hail Freedonia!” Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

webTitle: 9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa Bayoumi

fields.headline: 9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think
fields.trailText: Anti-Muslim sentiment is used as a political weapon. Meanwhile, Muslim American leaders are making a difference for all
fields.bodyText: It’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance. The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watch called “a severe wave of backlash violence”. A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, including at least three murders in the immediate backlash after the attacks. The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts soon compared to the Palmer Raids of the 1920s. The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating an episode of her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’an leapt on to the New York Times bestseller list that fall. Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims. One 2006 study found that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”. Much of this fear and ignorance has continued unevenly over the last quarter century, with negative attitudes towards Muslim Americans softening at times and hardening, sometimes into deadly violence, at other times. What’s interesting is when expressions of these attitudes happen. It turns out that predicting when animosity to Muslims will rise and fall may not be quite what you think. Researchers who study Islamophobia discovered several years ago that anti-Muslim outbreaks in the United States don’t follow highly publicized acts of terrorism. Rather, Islamophobic incidents tend to cluster more routinely around our election cycles. That’s what the New American Foundation found in 2018. That’s what the researcher Dalia Mogahed discovered earlier. And that’s partly what the Brookings Institution’s Shibley Telhami was referencing when he wrote, in 2024, that there was “strong suggestive evidence” that presidential messaging and crisis rhetoric can considerably sway American public attitudes toward Muslims. Islamophobia, in other words, is better understood not as an irrational fear of a religious other but rather as an increasingly instrumentalized part of our politics, one that is most often activated around our elections. (Needless to say, when Islamophobia is deployed, it’s at the expense of the American Muslim community’s wellbeing.) And since we’re also closing in on a fiercely contested midterm election season, we should take note of the sky-high levels of Islamophobic rhetoric we’re witnessing today from the (mostly Republican) politician class. Consider Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and Donald Trump’s close confidante. “Ban Muslims from holding office in America,” she posted on Twitter/X in July. Then there’s the South Carolina representative Nancy Mace, who wrote: “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic. We refuse to be silent.” The Florida representative Randy Fine, who has called for the deportation of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, believes: “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational.” And the senator Tommy Tuberville recently stated: “Michigan Democrats just voted to send a TERRORIST to the Senate. Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST who will do everything he can to destroy America.” In a thinly veiled Islamophobic comment, JD Vance recently said: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.” In Texas, the levels of Islamophobia are now stratospheric. Lone Star politicians loudly trumpet anti-Muslim messages and repeatedly introduce versions of anti-Muslim legislation, seeking to forbid everything from sharia courts, which don’t actually exist in Texas, to real estate developments by Muslims. Must be election season. The Texas governor Greg Abbott, who is up for re-election, has designated the country’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair), a foreign terrorist organization. This is ludicrous, of course, but as a Muslim organization, Cair’s an easy mark. As the Knight First Amendment Institute points out, “the domestic targeting of dissent starts with groups that those in power deem to be attractive political targets, but it never ends there. Without further opposition to these orders, CAIR is likely only the first of many groups to be in the crosshairs of politically motivated governors.” And that’s the larger point. Muslim Americans have been weathering these kinds of attacks for decades now, but what we also know is that attacks on Muslims won’t end as attacks on Muslims. For 25 years, we have known what it means to live under a national security state. We have known what warrantless surveillance feels like. We have known what politicized immigration enforcement looks like (remember the Muslim ban?). We have known what it means when our dissenting voices are silenced, especially when advocating for Palestine. And so, we recognize when those same tools are used by the National Security Agency to spy on ordinary Americans (as revealed by the whistleblower Edward Snowden) or when today’s mass deportations carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement resemble the immigration crackdown on Muslim immigrants decades earlier. Republicans worry loudly about their made-up fantasy of “creeping sharia”, but what all of us should really be concerned about is the reality of this creeping authoritarianism. Muslim Americans have hardly been silent when facing this repression. Instead, we’ve organized ourselves to oppose it. If the political culture of the United States is poised to deny us our legitimate rights, then the response must be preserving those rights for everybody, not just for Muslim Americans. That’s exactly what we’re witnessing today. Muslim Americans are more present in the American political scene than ever before. According to a recent study, a record 255 Muslims now serve in elected positions across the country, including 11 mayors, 18 judges and four members of the US House of Representatives. Muslim women account for more than 43% of the total. Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are probably today’s most visible Muslim American politicians. What makes them noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills, but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all. El-Sayed, for example, prioritizes universal access to healthcare and clean water, eliminating medical debt and banning corporate money in politics. Mamdani, for his part, has delivered a pilot program delivering taxpayer-funded childcare for two-year-olds, a rent freeze on rent-stabilized apartments, and a parents’ night out program, where children spend supervised time at city recreation centers so parents can have time for themselves. These Muslim politicians have discovered a simple, timeless truth: Democracy’s best defense is ensuring that everyone lives well. For the last 25 years, a bevy of political forces have routinely mobilized fear and ignorance against Muslim Americans to peddle the fiction that Muslims will take over the country. Their message has always been that Muslim Americans don’t belong in the United States. But you know what? We’re paying less attention to them by the hour. Muslim Americans have too much work to do preserving our democracy. The truth is that, while the Islamophobes waste everyone’s time with the ludicrous charge that Muslims and Americans are irreconcilably different, Muslim Americans are just too busy making a difference. For everyone’s sake. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

webTitle: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’

fields.headline: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’
fields.trailText: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise
fields.bodyText: Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May. As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances. Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again. That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs. The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade. Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed. “The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said. Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Evidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year. But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200. But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds. “We are approaching a crossroad,” he said. As economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance. Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient. “I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said. The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake. “They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.” The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today. Unleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump. Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out. Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz. But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel. “Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”

webTitle: Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfold

fields.headline: Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfold
fields.trailText: The world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home
fields.bodyText: As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.” A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant. “I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.” Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York, would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity, and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried. Speaking from Fairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post-9/11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart, and you visit it.” McPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants, and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad. McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.” Unspeakable loss On September 10, 2001 George W Bush travelled to Florida to push education reform legislation. AOL was seeking a big stake in AT&T’s cable unit. Promising tennis player Lleyton Hewitt, 20, had just swept Pete Sampras aside to win the US Open. America seemed unassailable. It had won the cold war and enjoyed a relatively peaceful 1990s as “the indispensable nation”, in secretary of state Madeleine Albright’s framing. From fiscal years 1998 to 2001, the federal government recorded four consecutive budget surpluses. But what had been dubbed “the American century” came to an apocalyptic end on the next morning. Nearly 3,000 people were killed as 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania. Among the most wrenching images were office workers leaping to their deaths from the burning twin towers. On the wall of the national September 11 museum in New York is a quotation from James Gilroy, a resident of lower Manhattan: “She had a business suit on, her hair was all askew … This woman stood there for what seemed like minutes, then she held down her skirt and then jumped off the ledge … I thought, how human, how modest, to hold down her skirt before she jumped.” Unthinkably, both of the 110-storey towers collapsed, unleashing giant clouds of ash and dust on the streets of lower Manhattan as fragments of paper fluttered down like confetti. David Blight, a historian who advised the museum, which opened in 2014, said: “It’s the most visual event in history – so photographed, so much footage, so many documentaries. It is so shocking, so horrifying that you can’t watch it without a certain weeping. One of the things that should never stop about 9/11 is the essential grief of it. There is a sheer sense of unspeakable loss.” At first the loss brought out America’s better angels. Firefighters and first responders displayed inspiring courage. Ordinary citizens queued to donate blood. The nation came together as rarely before and received global sympathy, with Russia pledging support, Iran holding candlelight vigils and Nato invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in its history. Bush visited Ground Zero in New York and, wielding a megaphone, declared that “the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon.” They did. The US invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaida and topple its Taliban protectors, a war that would drag on for a record 20 years only for the Taliban to return. Bush then attacked Iraq on the false premise that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction, at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives. The global war on terror expanded into a sprawling enterprise of military intervention, intelligence operations, detention and interrogation. Some suspects were tortured, including through waterboarding at CIA “black sites”. A quarter of a century later, 100 million Americans are too young to remember 9/11 and only from this vantage point, perhaps, can the consequences be seen clearly. Historians and policy experts interviewed by the Guardian suggest that the reaction to 9/11 was a profound strategic miscalculation that distracted the US from the rise of China and sowed the seeds of its own decline. Hunting for enemies “9/11 is when things began to go wrong for the United States,” suggested Bill Galston, a former policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The United States was at the apogee of its post-cold war power on September 10 and then, through a series of missteps and misjudgments on both the foreign and domestic front, we have thrown away a great deal of not only our power but our credibility. “In my judgment, 9/11 set off a quarter-century of misgovernment in the United States and we’ll pay the price for that for a very long time.” Did Osama Bin Laden, the al-Qaida leader who masterminded the attacks, win after all? If the metric of victory is measured by Bin Laden’s immediate, messianic desire to establish a global caliphate and expel all western presence from the Middle East, he evidently failed. Al-Qaida was eventually hunted to near-extinction and Bin Laden himself killed in a Pakistani compound in 2011. But if the terrorist’s success is measured by the magnitude of the self-inflicted wounds they provoke from their target, Bin Laden’s legacy is a slow, autoimmune decay within the US, it may have exceeded his darkest fantasies. Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser under Barack Obama, said: “Bin Laden in some ways failed in his intentions. He wanted the United States out of the Middle East. He wanted to topple certain governments in the Middle East. But in other ways 9/11 is the most successful terrorist attack in history insofar as it prompted such an overreach from the United States that we hastened our own decline, division and betrayal of our own story.” Like countless others, the course of Rhodes’ life was changed by 9/11. He was 23 and working on a city council election campaign at a polling site on the Brooklyn waterfront. He saw the second plane hit the twin towers and watched the rest of the carnage unfold. The event spurred him to move to Washington, and get involved in foreign policy. He regards the cost of 25 years of “forever wars” as incalculable. They placed a huge burden on the Americans who fought them and had to deal with problems ranging from war wounds to the opioids crisis. They also contributed to the destruction of the rules-based order, paving the way for Russia’s Vladimir Putin and others to reject the rules and use the language of counter-terrorism to justify stringent crackdowns. Then, there is the domestic sphere. Rhodes says the typical Fox News viewer during the Bush years was promised great victories over foreign enemies. “When nations don’t keep those types of promises, when you unleash that kind of nationalism and xenophobia and you don’t succeed on the battlefield, history tells you that people start to look for enemies within to blame,” he explained. “My experience in the Obama years is very much that ‘the other’ that had been constructed around terrorists morphed into the Black president or the immigrants crossing the southern border or LGBT people. The segments were the same but the enemy had changed to an enemy within.” Living with the legacy Donald Trump launched his first bid for the presidency, a decade ago, against the backdrop of this search for blame. Promoting the lie that Obama is a Muslim, demonising immigrants, and promising to build a border wall, he cut through by railing – in a clear break from Bush and Republican orthodoxy – against political elites for waging forever wars that he claimed he would stop (he has called the invasion of Iraq “the single worst decision ever made” in US history). “You’d never have Donald Trump as president without 9/11 because he basically stepped into that slipstream of othering people and captured the ugly xenophobia and nationalism that had been unleashed and the anger that people, particularly on the right, felt at being gaslit by the Bush administration for eight years,” said Rhodes. “It’s no coincidence that Trump’s ascent was marked by the destruction of Jeb Bush, who symbolised all those broken promises.” Now, Rhodes argues, the war on terror has come home. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are “basically running counter-insurgency strategies in American cities, with the same military equipment that we used to fight wars now in the hands of law enforcement”, he said. “Some of the same people have signed up to do it, and the same surveillance technologies that we use against terrorists abroad are now used against Americans. We are now living in the theatre of the war on terror and it’s obviously a source of growing discomfort to many Americans.” As the US overextended itself abroad, the machinery of endless war also boomeranged back on to the domestic front, eroding civil liberties and legal norms it claimed to defend. The Patriot Act, which dispensed with rules that prevented the state monitoring US citizens without “probable cause”, was passed just 45 days after the attacks, radically expanding the powers of law enforcement agencies. Jameel Jaffer, who moved to New York just weeks after the attacks before spending 14 years litigating national-security cases for the American Civil Liberties Union, saw the transition from the ground level. His early volunteer work involved visiting immigration detention centres in New York and New Jersey, where hundreds of immigrants had been rounded up in the panic after September 11. Over the next decade and a half, Jaffer litigated major constitutional battles involving warrantless wiretapping, secret detention and targeted killings. He watched as the National Security Agency developed an enormous surveillance apparatus, much of which became public through reporting and, later, Edward Snowden’s disclosures. Jaffer, now executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, argues that many of the surveillance authorities created after 9/11 remain in place or have become even more sweeping. “So much of what’s going on now is traceable to the institutions and authorities that were created after 9/11 and that the courts failed to limit,” he said. “The use of the material support laws to prosecute anti-ICE protesters in Texas. The use of the Espionage Act to threaten and intimidate journalists who are writing about issues that the public needs to know about. “Even the arrests and detentions and threatened deportation of students for protesting on university campuses: that policy is built on deference that the courts extended to the executive branch 25 years after 9/11. We are absolutely living with the legacy of these decisions made and policies instituted in the years after 9/11.” A new era Guantánamo Bay, where 780 men and boys have been imprisoned since 9/11, became one of the most visible symbols of the era. The Iraq war produced the Abu Ghraib scandal, in which US personnel and contractors subjected detainees to abuse, humiliation and torture. Obama tried, and failed, to shut down Guantánamo. Trump has since faced intense criticism for sending immigrants to the prison. Jeremy Varon, a history professor at the New School in New York and leading member of Witness Against Torture, a group seeking to close Guantánamo, said: “The United States committed to a programme and policy of torture, violating international law and its own laws, and an element of gratuitous cruelty and even sadism became operationally part of the war on terror. “People equated national strength and security with the ability to inflict harm on vulnerable others. The more violence we dish out, the stronger and the better and the safer we somehow are and a lot of that violence boomeranged and made new enemies. “But beyond those it victimised, it destroyed any pretence that we’re a constitutional order that obeys the rule of law, that honours national treaties. It inaugurated an era of executive power operating with utter impunity and immunity. The lawlessness of Trump is an utterly predictable consequence of the contempt for the rule of law, oversight, checks and balances that the Bush administration displayed.” For Varon, there is a clear connection between the brutal methods of the global war on terror and the excesses of ICE under Trump. He points to notorious detention centres in Texas and New Jersey where inmates routinely suffer medical neglect, and recent reports of harrowing deportation flights where migrants are flown to Africa in shackles. “People report living in fear and filth and squalor without access to basic hygiene, to attorneys,” he said. “Families are broken up and there’s a level of the willful infliction of suffering that is staggering and wouldn’t seem to be even a necessary part of the broad immigration strategy. “Again there’s this sick need that collectivities feel they have to dominate those that they perceive as lesser. Muslims and Arabs were the great community under suspicion and that’s been replaced to a large extent by brown-skinned migrants from other parts of the world. When you have a rhetoric that demonises people as criminal and subhuman, it invites their mistreatment.” A different path The collateral of this 25-year trajectory has been the evisceration of trust in US public institutions. Varon argues that this environment birthed a “post-truth condition” where empirical reality was abandoned and conspiracy theories thrive. The official September 11 narrative was challenged by the “truther” movement, which suggested the attacks were an “inside job” orchestrated by the US government. The Bush administration’s false claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction laid the groundwork for Trump’s cynical style, which relies on the public believing that everyone is lying so they might as well vote for a demagogue who is honest about it. Only last week it was reported that Trump has ordered the Department of Homeland Security, created in the aftermath of 9/11, to burnish his false claims of election fraud by embarking on a weeks-long search for non-citizens on US voter rolls, a move seen by watchdogs as an intimidation effort ahead of November’s midterm elections. The president will attend a commemoration at the Pentagon on Friday while JD Vance will be at the national 9/11 memorial in New York. Once again crowds will pause to remember the workers desperately waving clothes, sheets and tablecloths from the doomed towers, the firefighters who climbed staircases and never returned, the airline passengers who stormed the cockpit to stop United Airlines Flight 93 reaching its target in Washington. But will they weigh what came next, what it cost the US in blood and treasure and what might have happened if the country had chosen a different path? “Consider what we didn’t do,” said Rhodes. “I sometimes am haunted by this. The trillions of dollars spent on a forever war: what could that have been spent on? Climate change, universal healthcare, public education. There’s a real opportunity cost to how we chose to spend our time and resources. “If you came down to Earth from another planet and you had to make sense of the fact that the United States spent several trillion dollars chasing a relatively small number of terrorists around a few countries, toppling governments and then fighting insurgencies, when it has huge problems with deindustrialisation, with its education system, with the onset of climate change, you would think this is a country that has gone insane.”

webTitle: Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?

fields.headline: Friday briefing: Would a wealth tax save our public services or be billionaire repellent?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: Some think taxing the super-rich is a moral obligation, others say it drives cash away from the country. The truth may be somewhere in the middle
fields.bodyText: Morning pals, and let’s join in a heartfelt ευχαριστώ (thank you) to hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos for the estimated £330m he paid to the UK Treasury last year, and sadly won’t be contributing in future as he’s relocating to Greece. The publicity shy tycoon (and former Tory donor) has not made explicit his reasons for leaving the UK: so one can only speculate Rokos may be drawn by the noted health benefits of the Mediterranean diet, or the Greek government’s attractive €100,000 flat tax for overseas investors. Predictably, one man’s decision is now being framed by some as a dire warning to government to halt taxes on wealth in the UK. Conversely, campaigners are arguing ever more stridently for a specific wealth tax. With taxes already at their highest level since the second world war, could this be the goose to lay the cure-all golden egg and fix our crumbling public services? I spoke to our senior economics commentator, Aditya Chakrabortty, whose response might not be what you first expect it to be. And, yes, we get into goose-plucking too. Five big stories UK politics | Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs. Economy | Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. US news | JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success. Israel | Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. UK news | Consumers will pay higher energy bills unless the UK government speeds up work on a vast programme of upgrades to the electricity grid to enable the switch to renewables, the public spending watchdog has warned. In depth: We need to think about what wealth actually means Taxes are at record highs; satisfaction with public services at rock bottom. It’s a dichotomy familiar to us all from our own private focus groups, be that the street WhatsApp community or the bowling club. Alongside this, wealth is rising exponentially while wages are not: from 2000 to 2025, for example, average weekly earning rose just over 100% while property prices went up by about 240%. According to the British Social Attitudes Survey, the segment of the public who say the government should further increase taxes to spend more on health, education and welfare is at its lowest level in over a decade, at 36%. Aditya offers me a quote from Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the minister of finances under King Louis XIV of France: “The art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing.” “This has become harder to do as the tax burden has got higher,” Aditya tells me. “And so wealth taxes have really emerged as an attractive option to people in government, and to campaigners, not just here, but around western Europe and in America too.” *** What is a wealth tax and how would it work? Most advocates, when they talk about a wealth tax, mean an annual tax on assets over a certain threshold. The Green party of England and Wales, for example, proposes an annual tax of 1% on assets above £10m and 2% on those above £1bn, estimating it could raise almost £15bn a year. The campaign group Patriotic Millionaires – a bunch of likable sorts including Gary Lineker, Brian Eno and Val McDermid – suggests a 2% annual tax on total net wealth exceeding £10m, projecting revenue of £24bn a year. Oxfam, which is campaigning alongside them, says this rate would affect 20,000 people – about 0.04% of the UK population – and highlights polling carried out this May by YouGov, which found 76% of the public support “this fair wealth tax”. Campaigners present this as a slam dunk – minimal hissing for maximum feather. But dig into that polling a wee bit further and you’ll find the YouGov tracker poll, which instead indicates that Britons, over the past seven years, have a baseline preference for taxing income, rather than assets. It seems that, while the public are attracted to the concept of a wealth tax, they’re pretty selective about how wealth is defined. *** Why not start plucking? Critics of a wealth tax, in the right-of-centre thinktanks and the publications that report on them, argue that taxing the same wealth every year would penalise saving and investment; that a specific wealth tax would require expensive and unwieldy new administrative apparatus to value wealth; that focusing on the super-rich to raise revenue would make the UK a less attractive place for those people to work and invest. Aditya may not share their ideology, but he has his own reasons for being sceptical about current wealth tax campaigning, which he argues “offers apparently easy solutions, which will always affect someone else and never me”. Crucially, he says, if you’re running the government, the money raised by an annual wealth tax doesn’t make much dent in your bills, relatively speaking. The highest estimate is less than a third of the £80bn the UK government is planning to spend on defence annually by the end of the decade. And, once a tax is in place, so the dodges begin. “The one thing that the wealthy have in droves are advisers to show you how to avoid taxes.” “It doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it,” he adds, “just don’t oversell it as a magic bullet.” *** What’s this about a one-off wealth tax? So with that bubble burst, Aditya points us to what he considers the most substantial piece of work done on wealth taxes in the UK to date. A couple of academics and a tax barrister came together during Covid lockdown, when the rest of us were struggling with the recipe for banana bread, to form the independent Wealth Tax Commission. They propose a one-off wealth tax, arguing that its fairer because it targets people with the most ability to pay, is very difficult to avoid and wouldn’t distort behaviour because it’s one-time only. Accounting for behavioural responses and admin costs, they estimate this would raise a total of £260bn at a rate of 5% over £500,000 per individual, payable at 1% per year over five years. To be clear: this would be paid by individuals whose total wealth after mortgages and other debts, and after splitting the value of shared assets such as a jointly owned family homes, exceeded the tax threshold, and only on the value of wealth above that threshold. For example, a wealth tax levied at 1% above £500,000 would require a couple to have net wealth of more than £1m before any wealth tax would be payable. This is where Aditya gets excited: “£260bn is more than we get from income tax in a year. It would be transformative – you could put it in a sovereign wealth fund and invest in renewables. Or you could put it directly into the NHS and schools.” It would, however, affect a very different tranche of the population – those de facto millionaires with property in desirable parts of Edinburgh or Manchester or London. And that’s where the hissing starts up again. *** Are there other ways to tax wealth? We’ve heard it many times before over other proposed taxes on wealth: Rachel Reeves reversed her plans to end inheritance tax breaks for farmers after lobbyists drove tractors up to the doors of parliament and drowned out speeches with their horns. When Ed Miliband proposed a mansion tax on properties valued over £2m, to raise £1.2bn annually for the NHS, in his 2015 manifesto, he was eviscerated by the rightwing media, party critics and Myleene Klass, who confronted him in a TV debate, arguing the tax wouldn’t just touch the super-rich but would devastate “little grannies” who bought modest London homes that had simply skyrocketed in value over the decades. But times change, don’t they? And Reeves was able to avoid a similar backlash when she introduced a similar council tax surcharge on properties worth £2m or more at the last budget. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued consistently that, rather than introduce a new wealth tax, the government should sort out the mess of current capital and property taxes. In May, Wes Streeting received a mixed reception when he proposed equalising capital gains with income tax, as part of his brief tilt at Labour leadership, describing it as a “wealth tax that works”. And of course, HMRC could get better at collecting tax from the super-rich: its own estimates suggest that at least £2.1bn extra could be raised from closing the wealthy tax gap. The trouble with getting more granular on wealth taxation, Aditya says, is that many of the groups affected – whether that’s farmers, lawyers or GPs in partnerships – are also very well-networked and good at making a noise about the specific unfairness of targeting them as opposed to others. Which takes us back to the more subtle point about burden-sharing and democracy that underlies his arguments: by focusing on the billionaires in the corner, we avoid looking at the millionaires in the mirror – and having an honest conversation about what wealth is and how sophisticated those who have it are at lobbying against further taxes on it. An annual wealth tax has so much support right now because “it’s very politically palatable”, Aditya says. “It will poll brilliantly for you, because everyone will say that won’t affect them”. His advice is to pivot, philosophically: “Forget about the wealthy. Think about wealth.” We want to hear from you Remember the Makerfield test? Andy Burnham promised it would be at the heart of his decision-making: whether policy worked for areas, such as his constituency, that feel overlooked by Westminster. webTitle: ‘I’m on the ticket’: Trump implores Republicans to vote in November at unusual midterm convention

fields.headline: ‘I’m on the ticket’: Trump implores Republicans to vote in November at unusual midterm convention
fields.trailText: The president demonised Democrats in an attempt to wangle votes in midterms despite backlash over Iran war
fields.bodyText: With his approval rating at a historic low, Donald Trump has brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favour” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections. The president is facing a growing backlash over rising prices and the war in Iran. Sweeping losses for the Republican party could effectively turn Trump into a lame duck for his final two years in the White House. Sensing political danger, Trump wrapped up the novel two-day event in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday with a pitch that critics are likely to say smacked of desperation: “You gotta do me the biggest favour you’ve ever done me. You’ve gotta do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket! I’m on the ticket! He’s on the ticket! Pretend I’m on the ticket because this is going to turn out to be one of the most important elections.” In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the crowd of about 20,000 to raise their right hands and repeat: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way – I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.” The convention had been aimed at turning around Republicans’ fortunes. Opinion polls suggest they are on course to lose the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. In what was effectively an abridged version of his rambling keynote address on Wednesday, the president reiterated his promise of “Trump dividend” of $5,000 for every US adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. Democrats have dismissed the pledge as a bribe while economists have warned it would cost more than $1tn. Trump also hammered the theme of the convention: drawing a contrast between his own accomplishments and what he argues amounts to a threat posed by Democrats. “Less than two years ago, the American people gave us a mandate to save America – and in 19 months, I’ve delivered on every single promise I made,” he claimed. “They gave us wide open borders with 25 million people pouring in from all over the globe. They turned our cities into scenes of death and misery, murder, poverty and destruction, and made America a laughingstock all over world. “But we took that dark age of America and turned it into the golden age of America.” The reduction of prescription drug prices alone “should get us a big victory in our midterms”, he suggested, before he turned the microphone over to the opera performer Christopher Macchio, who belted out a soaring rendition of America the Beautiful as red, white, blue and golden balloons cascaded down from the ceiling of the basketball arena. The convention resembled a Trump mega-rally more than a traditional party meeting, with no nominations or formal business and more than 50 speakers or presentations each night. Supporters wore “Make America Great Again” regalia and waved signs displaying the Stars and Stripes. Republicans believe it has been successful in galvanising the party’s base in the face of stiff electoral headwinds. Earlier on Thursday, speaker after speaker sought to champion Trump’s accomplishments while constantly branding the Democratic party as extremist and communist. The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, delivered a fiery address setting Republican “common sense” against a “dystopian hellscape” of leftwing ideology. “As we speak, Democrat candidates across the country are openly embracing the radical ideology of democratic socialism,” suggested Trump Jr. “They claim that their socialism is for the people, but that’s the exact same story we’ve heard from every communist in human history.” Describing childhood memories of his grandparents in communist Czechoslovakia, he warned of bread lines and rationing. “Communism is on the march and it’s up to us to stop it in its tracks,” he said. Trump Jr framed the Republican platform, including pledges to end taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as a direct response to a “war on the working people” by Democrats. “The choice is clear,” he said. “Don’t let these radicals gaslight you into thinking common sense is extreme, and extreme is somehow common sense. Don’t let them convince you that caring about this country makes you a villain.” Senator Ted Cruz meanwhile warned of a “red-green alliance” between “communists and Islamists” who “hate Christians, hate Jews and hate capitalism”. Invoking his father’s escape from Cuban communism, Cruz declared that “sharia law has no place in America” and was “fundamentally inconsistent with the constitution”. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, echoed the conspiratorial tone, suggesting the nation was being “attacked from within”. The Democratic party is now beholden to radicals, he claimed, warning: “They’re the ones who have let the barbarians inside the gate, and next year the communists will be in Congress. That’s what’s so frightening.” Johnson added that, while big names like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are known entities, the bigger threat comes from “Democrats in the swing seats who say one thing, and then join forces and vote with the socialists that they’re afraid of”. The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, took the stage to champion the “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) platform. The son of a former US attorney general and nephew of John F Kennedy said the “irony of my presence here is inescapable”. He continued: “The Democrats of that era stood with labour and working people and the American middle class. Nearly every cop and firefighter was a Democrat … The Democratic party, in short, lost its way.” Speaking less than a mile from the spot where his uncle was assassinated in 1963, Kennedy claimed it was a “fact” that “neither my father, nor my uncle, would recognise the Democratic party of today”. JD Vance, the vice-president, gave the keynote address of the night. He said: “The Democrats are the party of hatred. They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it … America belongs to those who love it – not those who hate it.” The political attacks were briefly paused for two sombre interludes. A tribute marked one year since the assassination of the rightwing provocateur and organiser Charlie Kirk. Lucas Miles, a Turning Point USA vice-president, said that while “they could take the man, they could not take the mission”. Chants of “Charlie, Charlie” filled the air. The arena was plunged into darkness as Macchio performed Ave Maria on the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Two beams of light stretched upward from the arena floor, reminiscent of the twin towers in New York, as the crowd held up mobile phone lights. A video narration accompanying the tribute urged the audience to: “Say their names. Honour their sacrifice. Defend Freedom. Never forget September 11.” Democrats have dismissed the Republican event as a stunt. At a press conference in Dallas, Robert Garcia, a California congressman, told reporters: “What’s happening right now is Donald Trump is throwing a two-day party to celebrate himself, so that JD Vance can give a speech, and so his donors, some of whom have paid $800,000 a pop for these ticket packages, can spend two days celebrating themselves. “This is happening as the American public is struggling. So as Donald Trump and JD Vance party away for two days, the average American family can’t afford groceries, the cost of the rent’s going up, they’re looking at their gas prices skyrocketing and they’re making difficult choices at the dinner table. But Donald Trump does not care about the average American family or about affordability.”

webTitle: Trump doubles down on pledge of $5,000 payments if his party retains control of Congress on second night of convention – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump doubles down on pledge of $5,000 payments if his party retains control of Congress on second night of convention – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: Once again, the president tried to assuage the shock of oil prices increasing to more than $100 a barrel amid renewed hostilities with Iran. “The prices will go back to where they were,” he insisted. “The prices will go down to less than $2 a gallon for oil … I’m pretty sure. I’m pretty good at it.” A reminder that the average price for a gallon of gas is more than a dollar higher than before the war with Iran started in February. Trump also continued to praise JD Vance’s performance at the convention. “I think he did very well tonight, and he’s a very talented guy. He’s a great been a great vice-president. I think he did a very good job,” Trump said. Ahead of flying back to Washington, Trump told reporters on the tarmac that he isn’t pledging the $5,000 checks for every US adult to turn out the vote. “I did it as a reward,” he said, for “four years of horrible, a horrible situation caused by Biden”. Trump reiterated that the money, estimated to be well over $1tn, will come from tariff revenues and global investments. “We have growth like no country has ever seen before. We have trillions of dollars coming in, and that will end up being not a very big problem at all. And I think our people deserve it,” he said. Here are a few pictures as the second day of the GOP midterm convention wrapped up. The press pool notes that Donald Trump has now boarded his flight from Dallas, back to Washington. Donald Trump doubled down on his pledge to pay all US adults $5,000 if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge tonight, as many lawmakers and officials – including his vice-president, JD Vance – avoided mentioning the so-called “dividend” altogether. Trump defended his plan: “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars.” In a shorter address to voters than his nearly two-hour speech on Wednesday, Trump again pleaded with voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” in November. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump also told those gathered in Dallas that they would “go to hell” if they didn’t vote. Earlier, JD Vance urged Republicans who may oppose parts of the Trump administration’s agenda not to abandon the party in November’s congressional races. The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming. Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office. Other cabinet officials and Trump allies addressed the crowd at the hastily organized convention in Dallas. Throughout the night we heard from health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who said the “irony” of his “presence here is inescapable” – a former Democrat from a political dynasty. “I mourn the fact that neither my father nor my uncle would recognize the Democratic party of today,” Kennedy said. Meanwhile, Karoline Leavitt, the former White House secretary, said it felt “much better speaking to a stadium full of patriots than a briefing room full of journalists”. Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway. Also today, Trump said that he doesn’t think that Congress would need to approve the $5,000 checks that he wants to cut should Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. “The country is doing so well, we’ve taken in trillions of dollars in tariffs and other things,” the president said in an interview with CBS News – inflating the revenue generated from the duties he’s implemented. However, any money generated from tariffs is deposited to the US treasury, and then allocated by Congress through legislation. Earlier, we reported that Joseph diGenova, the longtime Trump loyalist hired in April to pursue the “grand conspiracy” charges against the president’s perceived enemies such as former CIA director John Brennan, resigned today. I called diGenova and he said pointedly that “sometimes people want things done faster and that’s all you can do”. He appeared to be referring to concerns among other Trump loyalists that Trump’s retribution cases weren’t moving quickly enough. “The bottom line is it takes a long time to make good cases, and you simply have to work at it. And, you know, sometimes people want things done faster, and that’s all you can do. All you can do is do the best you can under the circumstances,” diGenova added. Retribution by the justice department against Trump’s perceived adversaries has been one of the president’s highest priorities. Though diGenova’s comments to the Guardian clearly hint at dissent and disagreement inside the justice department over the cases, he declined to spell out exactly why he quit. “I’m not going to make any comments about indictments or anything else. When you’ve been a prosecutor as long as I have. You know how to make cases, and it takes time. And that’s just part of the process. And sometimes that works out, and sometimes it doesn’t,” he said. During the first Trump administration, diGenova was a legal adviser to far-right journalist John Solomon, who has played an official role in White House efforts to push the conspiracy allegations. Trump’s energy for talking about politics appears to have waned. “I’ve been doing this now for seven days straight. I want a little music, if you don’t mind,” Trump said, while introducing opera singer Christopher Macchio. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump added: “You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell.” Trump said that voters have to do “the biggest favor you’ve ever done me” and “pretend I’m on the ticket”. “In a way I am on the ballot,” the president said, despite the fact that many Republicans in battleground states might actually be hampered by yolking themselves to the Trump administration, amid record low approval ratings. Trump acknowledged that when he’s on the ticket “everybody comes to vote”, but it is still crucial to vote for Republicans in races across the country. He urged Republicans to turn out and vote for Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for US Senate in Texas. Once again, Trump took digs at Paxton’s appearance, and even revealed that many advisers pleaded with him to not offer comment. “I don’t really like the way he looks, I don’t like it,” Trump said. “But you know what I do like? He was the greatest attorney general in the history of Texas.” The president just mentioned the $5,000 for all US adults he has promised if Republicans win the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge on stage tonight. “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars,” Trump said. The major legal question of whether this “dividend” actually violates federal law still remains. As he runs through what he sees as his main achievements, Trump repeats his false claim that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has delivered the “largest tax cuts in American history”. This isn’t true. In fact, these tax cuts aren’t actually in the top five in US history. Trump praised Vance for his performance on stage, and repeated claims that the venue is “packed” again. He said he would be “a little bit brief” in his remarks because of his nearly two-hour speech last night. “I don’t feel like going over the same material again,” the president said. Donald Trump is, again, walking on stage to a second live performance of God Bless the USA by Lee Greenwood. As Vance wraps up his remarks, insisting that it’s imperative to send Democrats “packing” in November, the vice-president was another speaker who avoided mentioning Trump’s $5,000 “dividend” to every US adult if Republicans hold on to control of Congress. Interestingly, Vance doubled down on his criticism of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, by chiding him for appearing to suggest that Vance’s grandfather (who helped raised him) wouldn’t approve of the vice-president’s interracial marriage. “The Democrats are the party of hatred. They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it,” Vance said. “They say that people with names like James Vance are incapable of loving people with names like Usha, and they couldn’t be more wrong.” Vance continued to urge voters to stay with the Republican party. “We have done a lot, my friends, and we can do a lot more if we fight together,” he said. “Let’s send these lunatics packing and govern our country for the future.” JD Vance just used Charlie Kirk as his vehicle to implore voters who may disagree with certain Trump administration policies not to abandon the party in key congressional races this November. “Charlie hated war. Whether it was Europe or Africa, the Middle East, he didn’t care. He just hated war. That was his view. Now, of course, there are people who love what we’ve done and people who don’t,” Vance said, referring to the ongoing conflict in Iran that has caused prices across the country to spike. “What I’m asking you to do is do what Charlie did: do not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Don’t don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.” Vance is now slamming several Democratic nominees in states where Republicans are facing key challenges. This includes James Talarico in Texas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan – both of whom are frequent targets of the GOP ahead of November. “These are the candidates that congressional Democrats have put forth for you to vote for in November,” the vice-president said. “They asked my friends for a one-way ticket to Washington to legislate and regulate and wield power over your lives. Instead, in my opinion, they need a one-way ticket to a mental hospital.” In many ways this speech is an audition for JD Vance’s possible 2028 presidential run. He’s spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office. Vance just acknowledged that a protester interrupted his remarks while waving a Mexican flag. “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket,” Vance said, in a moment that was red meat for the base, and saw chants of “USA” erupt throughout the arena. Vance, using the birth of his fourth child as a launchpad, addressed “radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families all across our country” to “stay the hell away from our kids”. A quick aside from Vance, who says that his wife – Usha – who gave birth to a son over a month ago, is not in Dallas. The vice-president recalled that his wife said “hell no” when Republican National Committee (RNC) organizers asked if she would be willing to introduce her husband, just two weeks after giving birth. “But she sends her love, and I know she’s watching at home,” Vance said. JD Vance has dedicated a portion of his speech, as we noted earlier, to remember Charlie Kirk – the Turning Point USA founder who was murdered at a campus event in Utah exactly a year ago. Vance and Kirk were close friends. “Charlie left behind two children, two little kids … I hope that one day they will watch and they will know, and they will understand what I’m trying to say to them tonight. Though they may not appreciate it today, history will record that your father was a great man,” Vance said. In his opening remarks, Vance said that Republicans in the arena today are not going to let the US “go backwards”. The vice-president noted that voters were “tired” two years ago. “We were tired of not being able to afford anything,” Vance added; even though inflation is actually higher than it was when Joe Biden left office in 2025. Vice-president JD Vance has just walked out on stage at Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “I gotta say, it’s pretty cool to hear a crowd that is this fired up chant your name. So go ahead and do it again,” Vance said. As he wrapped up his speech, Donald Trump Jr repeated a common refrain we’ve heard across both nights of the GOP midterm convention. “The choice is clear,” he said. “Don’t let these radicals gaslight you into thinking common sense is extreme, and extreme is somehow common sense. Don’t let them convince you that caring about this country makes you a villain.” The president’s son added: “Not a single one of us can afford to sleep through the midterms.” On stage, there has been little to no mention of Donald Trump’s pledge to pay all adult US citizens $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. Instead, most of the speakers have focused on Charlie Kirk’s murder a year ago today, bashing Democrats and progressive candidates on the ballot in November and trying to focus on how the administration is tackling the issue of affordability. Donald Trump Jr has spent much of his speech re-hashing many of the hard-right talking points of the night. “As we speak, Democrat candidates across the country are openly embracing the radical ideology of democratic socialism,” the president’s son said. “They claim that their socialism is for the people, but that’s the exact same story we’ve heard from every communist in human history.” Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, is now speaking to Republicans at the second night of the midterm convention. “It feels good to be back behind a podium,” Leavitt said. “It feels much better speaking to a stadium full of patriots than a briefing room full of journalists.” A reminder that the former press secretary left the West Wing to spend more time with her family (she recently gave birth to her second child) and take a role at the Trump-aligned Super Pac, Maga Inc. Dallas mayor Eric Johnson is now addressing attendees at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas. A reminder that Johnson was, until recently, a Democrat. He became a registered Republican in 2023. “Today’s progressives don’t believe in giving hardworking Americans a square deal, a fair deal, or a new deal,” Johnson told the crowd. “Every time these extreme democrat socialists grab power, all we get is a raw deal.” As part of his breakneck midterm race tour, Donald Trump will travel to North Carolina next to help campaign on behalf of Michael Whatley, the Republican nominee in the state’s race for US Senate. The president will deliver remarks in Gastonia, Whatley’s hometown, on Wednesday. Kennedy hurled one of many attacks against transgender people of the night during his speech. Robert F Kennedy Jr also spoke about his uncle, Ted Kennedy, who served as a senator for Massachusetts and fought for several amendments to Title IX – which prohibits sex-based discrimination in any educational program that receives federal funding. “He [Ted Kennedy] wanted to make sure that women, real women, were able to have a safe and guaranteed spot in college sports,” the health secretary said. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, is now addressing the crowd in Dallas. He’s outlining his shift from a staunch Democrat to an independent, and eventually working for a Republican administration. “The irony of my presence here is inescapable,” Kennedy said, acknowledging that he hails from a political dynasty that includes his father (and namesake), who served as the US attorney general and a Democratic senator. “The Democrats of that era stood with labor and working people and the American middle class. Nearly every cop and firefighter was a Democrat,” Kennedy added. “I mourn the fact that neither my father nor my uncle would recognize the Democratic Party of today.” As we noted earlier, dozens of protesters have gathered outside the arena where the GOP midterm convention is taking place. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway. Vice-president JD Vance will talk about fatherhood and his populist vision in his midterm convention speech, a source familiar with the address told Agence France-Presse (AFP). Vance will also reflect on the death of Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist who was assassinated exactly a year ago, the source told AFP.
